title: No Way!
subtitle: Four ways to say you can't believe it
review: Text and notes written by Claude, from the author's own childhood stories: check them. No Burmese yet.
intro: An angel expected in the garden, a lemon syrup that gets thinner in the sun, a dangerous belly button and a great debate between six-year-olds: four true stories from a childhood in Yangon, told by Emma. Listen for how Lucas shows he cannot believe it, and how Emma insists that it is true.

lines.text: You're not going to believe this. When I was five, my mother said an angel was coming.
lines.note: You're not going to believe this: say it before a surprising story.

lines.text: Really?
lines.note: Really? The simplest way to show surprise.

lines.text: To our garden. But only if we were quiet. Angels are shy.
lines.note: Shy: not comfortable with people. Only if = on one condition.

lines.text: Seriously? And you believed her?
lines.note: Seriously? = is that really true? Believed: past of believe.

lines.text: Four kids. Two hours. Not a sound.
lines.note: Not a sound = total silence.

lines.text: No kidding. Did the angel come?
lines.note: No kidding = I am surprised, but I believe you.

lines.text: No. My brother sneezed.
lines.note: Sneezed: past of sneeze. Achoo!

lines.text: My mother made lemon syrup. Weeks in the sun, thick and golden.
lines.note: Syrup: a thick, sweet liquid. Thick: not like water.

lines.text: Sounds good.
lines.note: Sounds good = I like the idea.

lines.text: A neighbor tried it. Her syrup got thinner every week.
lines.note: Got thinner: became more like water. Thin, thinner.

lines.text: Thinner? That's impossible.
lines.note: That's impossible: it cannot happen.

lines.text: That's what she said. My mother said, "Ask your kids."
lines.note: Ask your kids: the mother knows who did it.

lines.text: No way. They drank it?
lines.note: No way! = I cannot believe it. Drank: past of drink.

lines.text: And filled the bottle with water. Every day.
lines.note: Filled: past of fill.

lines.text: Unbelievable. How did your mother know?
lines.note: Unbelievable! = very hard to believe.

lines.text: She had us.
lines.note: She had us: she had children like that too.

lines.text: When I was five, my mother told me where babies come from.
lines.note: Where babies come from: how babies are made.

lines.text: And?
lines.note: And? = go on, tell me.

lines.text: The King touches the Queen's belly button.
lines.note: Belly button: the small round mark on your stomach.

lines.text: You're kidding.
lines.note: You're kidding = you are joking; that is not true.

lines.text: I swear. So I stopped wrestling with my brothers. Too dangerous.
lines.note: I swear = I promise it is true. Wrestling: fighting for fun.

lines.text: You can't be serious.
lines.note: You can't be serious = I think you are joking.

lines.text: I'm not lying. I protected my belly button for years.
lines.note: I'm not lying = it is true. Protected: kept safe.

lines.text: Are you kidding me? So if I just…
lines.note: Are you kidding me? Stronger than You're kidding.

lines.text: Don't even think about it.
lines.note: Don't even think about it = do not try.

lines.text: One day, the boy next door said babies come from their mother's bottom.
lines.note: The boy next door: the boy from the neighbors' house. Bottom: the part of the body you sit on.

lines.text: He said what? That's crazy!
lines.note: He said what? Repeat with what when you cannot believe what you heard. That's crazy!

lines.text: That's what I told him. "Nonsense! Babies come from the tummy."
lines.note: Nonsense! = that is not true and it is silly. Tummy: a child's word for stomach.

lines.text: And he believed you?
No. He said, "Yeah, right." We argued for twenty minutes.
lines.note: Yeah, right: you say yes, but you mean no. Argued: past of argue.

lines.text: Holy cow. Who won?
lines.note: Holy cow! shows big surprise. Informal. Won: past of win.

lines.text: I did. I said, "Fine. You came from the bottom. We came from the tummy."
lines.note: Fine = OK, I will not argue any more.

lines.text: And you were five?
Six. And very sure of myself.
lines.note: Sure of myself = certain that I was right.

lines.text: Some things never change.
lines.note: Some things never change: she is still like that.

notes: Really? Seriously? No kidding? show surprise and ask the speaker to go on.
You're kidding. You can't be serious. Are you kidding me? say: I think this is a joke.
That's impossible. No way! Unbelievable! say: this cannot be true.
That's crazy! and Holy cow! are informal, for a big surprise.
Yeah, right and Nonsense! say that you do not believe the other person at all.
To answer: I swear. I'm not lying. Believe me. And before a surprising story: You're not going to believe this.
The stories use the simple past: said, believed, drank, filled, stopped, argued, won.

questions.q: Your friend says: “I saw a monkey on the bus.” You are surprised. What do you say?
questions.why: Really? shows surprise. I swear is what your friend can answer.
You're kidding = you are joking; I cannot believe it.

questions.q: Nobody believes your story, but it is true. What do you say?
questions.why: I swear = I promise it is true.

questions.q: “I'll clean my room tomorrow.” “Yeah, right.” Does the second person believe it?
questions.why: Yeah, right is ironic: the words say yes, the voice says no.

questions.q: Which word is the past of drink?
